newsitem.title: FRANCE: Lyonnaise, Suez confirm merger talks. [CORRECTED 16:20 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Lyonnaise, Suez confirm merger talks. [CORRECTED 16:20 GMT]

text.p: French holding company Cie de Suez and utilities group Lyonnaise des Eaux confirmed on Friday they were holding merger talks and said their boards would meet on April 11 to consider a merger plan.

In a brief statement the two companies noted that the Suez and Lyonnaise boards would meet as planned on April 1 and April 2 respectively to approve 1996 results and then be called back for special meetings on April 11 "to discuss a merger plan between the two companies".
The joint statement gave no more details and spokesmen at both companies declined all further comment.
It came after more than a week of intense market and newspaper speculation that the two companies were working all out to finalise a merger plan.

A merger of the two -- Lyonnaise, with its sprawling empire in water distribution, electricity and construction, and Suez, a conglomerate searching for a raison d'etre after selling investment bank Indosuez and other key assets-- would make sense, according to stock market analysts.
A tie-up would solve the identity crisis for cash-rich Suez and could provide Lyonnaise with the resources it needs to keep up with expanding rival Generale des Eaux, they say.
Together the two would form a group ranking in France's top ten companies, still a touch behind Generale des Eaux, in terms of market capitalisation.

The firms affected by any deal through their shareholdings or involvement in the sector include a number of major players such as Generale des Eaux itself, which has an indirect stake in Suez through a 20 percent holding in Belgian Electrafina. (Corrects to remove erroneous reference to Electrabel.)
Despite reports of serious worries at Generale des Eaux, the group has denied it would try to block a Lyonnaise/Suez tie-up by launching a counter-bid for Suez.

Other Suez shareholders such as insurer Axa-UAP have declined to comment, while the cooperative banking giant Credit Agricole has refused to go further than the comment by chairman Lucien Douroux this week that "we are following the current situation with interest".
He said his bank's 8.5 percent Suez stake was a "strategic investment". It also has 3.3 percent of Lyonnaise.

But the ramifications are not purely of French stock market interest. Belgian Prime Minister went on record recently to say he was concerned that any merger should not damage the autonomy of Tractebel, owner of Electrabel.
In the complex matrix of crossed shareholdings, Suez owns 63 percent of Societe Generale de Belgique, which in turn controls Tractebel.

Suez, which has sold off assets like Indosuez and has been shoring up its accounts after heavy losses when the property market collapsed in the early 1990s, made a net attributable loss of 3.96 billion francs in 1995. Lyonnaise profit in the same year fell to 906 million from 1.06 billion francs.
